data.title: Ducové – Kostolec: a Great Moravian magnate's court above the Váh
data.excerpt: A limestone promontory rising 70–80 m above the Váh floodplain between Ducové and Hubina carries one of the most remarkable early medieval sites in Slovakia: a Great Moravian magnate's court with a stone rotunda, the best-preserved building surviving from Great Moravia. Behind its oak palisade lived no more than 60–70 people, and after the court burned down the little church went on serving a cemetery that grew here until the middle of the 15th century.
data.metaTitle: Ducové-Kostolec – a Great Moravian court above the Váh
data.metaDescription: On a limestone promontory above the Váh, the Slavic elite built a court with a rotunda in the 9th century — the hillfort of Ducové-Kostolec.

keyFacts.label: Rotunda
keyFacts.value: Over 12 m long (including the apse), almost 9 m wide, walls surviving to over 7 m — the best-preserved building from the territory of Great Moravia

keyFacts.label: Identical ground plan
keyFacts.value: Matching dimensions with the rotunda at Nitrianska Blatnica and with one of the rotundas at Mikulčice

keyFacts.label: Palisade
keyFacts.value: Oak beams (20–25 cm) set in lime mortar, about 2.5 m high; the highest point of the defences stood about 10 m above the bottom of the ditch

keyFacts.label: Internal division
keyFacts.value: Three inner palisades separating the small church with its cemetery, the lord's log dwellings and the quarters of the warband

keyFacts.label: Tomb beside the rotunda
keyFacts.value: About 25 graves cut into the rock; a separate rock-cut tomb 2 m deep held a youth and an adult man in coffins

keyFacts.label: Type of residence
keyFacts.value: According to A. Ruttkay, similar in form to the Frankish courts (curtis) of the 8th–9th centuries; an ‘external’ court outside the Great Moravian power centres

keyFacts.label: Today
keyFacts.value: A national cultural monument since 1990, with an indicative reconstruction of the palisade, gateway and building foundations — one of the few hillforts in Slovakia treated this way

timeline.title: The earliest Eneolithic occupation
timeline.description: Finds from the earliest phase of the Channelled Ware culture, Bošáca group.

timeline.title: A hillfort of the Velatice culture
timeline.description: The people of the Velatice culture built an important hillfort on the terrace of Kostolec, with a massive rampart and ditch that survive to this day; inhumation and cremation graves were also recorded.

timeline.title: Temporary occupation in the Roman period
timeline.description: Small finds of this period come from the site.

timeline.title: A magnate's court
timeline.description: Defences of an oak palisade, log dwelling houses and a rotunda were built — the seat of members of the court aristocracy; no more than 60–70 people ever lived inside the defences.

timeline.title: The demise of the court
timeline.description: Its demise may be linked to the ambitions of the Árpáds as they extended the territory they had occupied.

timeline.title: The rotunda outlives the court
timeline.description: The small church went on serving even after the palisade and the log buildings had gone, although the new cemetery no longer respected its ground plan.

timeline.title: A medieval cemetery
timeline.description: The area of the former court was used as a cemetery — excavation uncovered 1,545 graves (1,900 according to Dvořák), a Slovak record for the number of excavated graves at a single site.

timeline.title: A Hussite military post
timeline.description: A military base was built on Kostolec, probably in connection with the activity of the Brethren armies in the Váh region; occupation of this period was also identified at the locality known as Bašta.

timeline.title: Rescue excavation
timeline.description: Prompted by the threat of quarrying for the raw material used to make brizolit render.

timeline.title: Large-scale systematic excavation
timeline.description: The results led to the quarrying being moved elsewhere (from 1973) and later to the creation of an open-air display with an indicative reconstruction (from 1976).

timeline.description: The Kostolec site was declared a national cultural monument.

children.text: The hillfort of Ducové-Kostolec occupies a limestone-and-dolomite promontory, visible from far away and rising 70–80 m above the Váh floodplain between the villages of Ducové and Hubina, directly above the road from Piešťany to Beckov. The summit of Kostolec bears a plateau c. 0.75 ha in area, enclosed on the northern side by a massive neck rampart dating from the Late Bronze Age. A wide ditch ran along the outer side of the rampart. In the 9th century representatives of the Slavic elite made use of this favourable terrain, set directly above the river floodplain, to build a residence — a court with a trapezoidal ground plan, c. 0.5 ha in size.

blocks.caption: The appearance of the court in the 9th–10th centuries (Ing. Kyjovská)
blocks.alt: The appearance of the court in the 9th–10th centuries (Ing. Kyjovská)

children.text: From the archaeological and historical point of view, the hill of Kostolec ranks among the important Slavic sites. It is protected by the status of a national cultural monument. Further occupation at the locality of Kostolec has been identified in the late phase of the Neolithic — the Eneolithic. It belongs to the earliest phase of the Channelled Ware culture, Bošáca group (2600 BC). Finds from the locality known as Cintorín-Veľký diel belong to the Lengyel culture (4000–3000 BC). A stone axe found in the past within the built-up area of the village is also broadly dated to the Neolithic. In the Late Bronze Age (1300–1100 BC) the people of the Velatice culture built an important hillfort on the terrace of Kostolec. The hillfort's fortification system — a massive rampart and ditch — survives at the site to this day. Besides the settlement, inhumation graves of members of the Velatice culture were also identified at Kostolec. Cremation graves of the same period were found in the past in the upper part of the village of Ducové and at the localities known as Veľký diel and Panský járok. Kostolec was also temporarily occupied in the Roman period (the 2nd–3rd centuries AD), and small finds come from the site.

The most significant occupation of Kostolec in terms of Slovak national history is the Slavic occupation of the 9th–10th centuries. The defences that were built — a palisade of oak posts — together with the residential buildings, log houses, and the small church, a rotunda, are characterised as parts of a magnate's court, the seat of members of the court aristocracy. The modern indicative reconstruction gives a good idea of how they were laid out on the ground. The demise of the court may be linked to the ambitions of the Árpáds as they extended the territory they had occupied at the end of the 10th century. After the court was finally abandoned, its area was used as a cemetery until the middle of the 15th century. During the archaeological excavation carried out in 1968–1972 and 1975, 1,545 graves containing the material culture of the time were uncovered in the medieval cemetery. In the middle of the 15th century, probably in connection with the activity of the Hussite Brethren armies in the Váh region, a military post — a base — was built on Kostolec. Occupation of the 15th century was also identified at the locality known as Bašta.

children.text: Pavel Dvořák deals with the magnate's court at Ducové in a most engaging way in his book Stopy dávnej minulosti 3 (Traces of the Distant Past 3: The Birth of a Nation). I shall take the liberty of quoting a few sentences from this remarkable work.

"Archaeological excavation uncovered on the crown of Kostolec a trapezoidal area of about half a hectare, protected by a steep rocky scarp interrupted in only two places: by a narrow, easily guarded neck on the north, and on the opposite side by a gently rising meadow, up which one can today drive comfortably to Kostolec even in a car. These were the weak points of the defences, and this is why a high rampart and a ditch were raised here. They were built by people back in prehistory, in the Bronze Age; the Great Moravian builder merely cleaned out the ditch, repaired the rampart and set a palisade on its crest. The highest point of the defences stood about ten metres above the bottom of the ditch, which was an enormous advantage for a defender who had any attacker far below him. The palisade was massive, built of thick (20 to 25 centimetres) hewn oak beams driven into the ground and set in lime mortar. Judging by the impressions in the mortar, the beams stood about two and a half metres high. A massive gateway, likewise of oak beams, led through the palisade. Behind it stood a stone church with a small cemetery around it. A second, inner palisade separated it from the fortress, and the space behind that was divided in two by a third palisade. Two log buildings stood in the larger part. The larger of them had three rooms with a floor of poured mortar, in which the outlines of the oak beams of the outer walls, 14 to 16 centimetres thick, and of thinner internal partitions were impressed. The mortar preserved impressions of the interior fittings, of furniture, and a tangle of small holes that is hard to decipher; only a hinge and a nail by one of the walls speak more clearly: perhaps a chest stood there. Beside the house there was a taller tower-like structure, perhaps a refuge in moments of greatest danger. Both buildings were heated by stone fireplaces with a side flue for the smoke, which was a luxury in those days. Behind the second palisade was a third, which separated the lord of Kostolec from his soldiers, his warband. Traces of a building were found here too, unfortunately only indistinct ones, from which it is hard to read anything more precise.

blocks.caption: The palisade, the gateway and the foundations of the Great Moravian church
blocks.alt: The palisade, the gateway and the foundations of the Great Moravian church

children.text: No more than 60–70 people ever lived inside the defences, so this was not a large hillfort for everyone, as at Pobedim, for hundreds and sometimes even thousands of people, but a fortified court, a forerunner of the castle, the seat of a magnate and his retinue. No traces of craft working, typical of Great Moravian hillforts, were found here, for example. This is evidence of a change in society: the feudal lord — the warrior — separated himself from those who fed him and moved into his own fortified space. It is a change that came from the more advanced west, from the Frankish Empire.

The separation of the rulers from the common world is also attested by the church, a rotunda more than twelve metres long (including the apse) and almost nine metres wide. It was a private church, the property of the feudal lord, with space for the lord and his retinue. The rotunda from Ducové is the best-preserved building from the territory of Great Moravia. Not only its foundations survive, but also pieces of walls plastered on both sides and even painted on the inside. It is a perfect masterpiece: the walls of the church consisted of a thin stone shell that rose to a height of more than seven metres.

children.text: Around the church there used to be a small cemetery, some twenty-five graves cut deep into the rock, one beside another, with a path winding between the graves from the church to the inner part of the palisade. The graves mostly held men with spurs and fighting knives, their clothing fastened at the knees in the riding fashion; a few women were given gold and silver in the grave. In a separate rock-cut tomb about two metres deep lay two people, a youth and an adult man, in coffins placed against opposite walls."

Alexander Ruttkay, in his paper VÝZNAMNÉ ARCHEOLOGICKÉ LOKALITY Z VČASNÉHO STREDOVEKU V OBLASTI POVAŽSKÉHO INOVCA (Important early medieval archaeological sites in the Považský Inovec area), states that:

"The court on Kostolec is similar in form to the Frankish courts (curtis) of the 8th–9th centuries, especially to their presumed upland forms with a ‘shield-shaped’ ground plan. Specific features of the social development of the Slavs north of the Danube in the 9th century are reflected here, however. This is an ‘external’ court outside the area of the Great Moravian power centres, the private residence of a local representative of the aristocracy with a small armed retinue. The administrative, residential and representative function of the site within its micro-region was reinforced by its advantageous military and strategic position above a river ford. The church, with links above all to the Aquileian sphere in northern Italy, is evidence of Christianising currents other than the Byzantine mission of the brothers from Thessalonica."

children.text: On the demise of the court Dvořák writes: "Kostolec even survived two watershed changes: the fall of Great Moravia and the defeat of the Old Hungarians at the Lech. Perhaps it too had become superfluous; Beckov Castle, which lies a short way upstream along the Váh, in a narrow gap between the hills, almost suggests itself as a replacement.

Anything is possible, but only one thing is certain: the little church did not perish, it outlived even the last lord of Kostolec. It went on serving after the ruin of the lord's court. For is it not strange that no one robbed or desecrated the rich graves? Evidently because burial did not cease here even after the fire; on the contrary, more graves were added, poor and rich, shallow and deep. And this is the moment of the boulders we spoke of at the beginning. Large flat stones were laid over the new dead, taken not only from Kostolec itself but also brought from places tens of kilometres away, where the deceased had lived. This went on until the middle of the 15th century. Nineteen hundred excavated graves is a Slovak record, if records were kept in such a field. True, the new cemetery no longer respected the palisade; the graves cut across it and intrude into its foundations, and evidently not a trace of it was left. But the little church stood at least until the 11th century; it outlived both the palisade and the log buildings"

A remarkable point to which Dvořák draws attention in his book is that the Kostolec rotunda has exactly the same ground plan (in its dimensions), including the apse, as the rotunda at Nitrianska Blatnica, which still stands today and is used for services — unfortunately not in its original Romanesque form, but rebuilt in the Baroque style. It also has the same ground plan as one of the rotundas whose foundations were uncovered at Mikulčice.

A rescue excavation was carried out at Kostolec in 1968 and a large-scale systematic excavation in 1969–1975, at a time when the quarrying of the good-quality local raw material used to make brizolit render threatened the site with almost inevitable rapid and complete destruction. From 1973 the results of the excavation led first to the quarrying being moved elsewhere, then to a partial tidying-up and, yes, also to the ‘completion’ of damaged parts of the site; from 1976 to the creation of an open-air display with an indicative reconstruction of the most important excavated features; and finally, in 1990, to the site being declared a national cultural monument.

children.text: Ducové is one of the very few hillforts in Slovakia where at least a partial reconstruction of the original palisade defences has been carried out. Unfortunately the palisade is gradually decaying and clearly no one looks after the court. The information panels have also seen their days of glory come and go, and worst of all is the signposting of the access route to the hillfort, which is literally detective work. Such an attitude on the part of the village and of the responsible parties — the owners of the site (I believe it is the church) — is really hard to understand.

Drive through the village of Ducové and, shortly before its end, a shabby signboard overgrown with bushes sticks out on the left of the main road, pointing the way to the hillfort. So turn left off the main road and continue along a broken-up track that will bring you right up to the ramparts of the hillfort. It is possible to get there by car as well. At the hillfort, as is well known, there are indicative reconstructions of the palisade, the gateway and the foundations of the buildings, as well as the foundations of the Great Moravian rotunda. The information panels there are new now and nicely done. We shall see whether the civic association ‘
’ manages to carry out good-quality reconstructions of the dwellings, or perhaps of the defensive wall, on the site.
